spec.credit: UPSC CSE (Main) 2017 · General Studies Paper II · Q12
spec.text: Examine the scope of Fundamental Rights in the light of the latest judgement of the Supreme Court on Right to Privacy.

scenes.vo: UPSC, twenty seventeen. General Studies Paper Two, fifteen marks, two hundred and fifty words. Examine the scope of Fundamental Rights in the light of the latest privacy judgment. Here is the twist. The judgment did not amend anything. It found a right already there.
scenes.visual: The printed question on a paper card, credit line 'UPSC CSE (Main) 2017, GS Paper II, Q12'. The words 'scope of Fundamental Rights' glow faintly (plant).

spec.text: Examine the scope of Fundamental Rights in the light of the latest judgement of the Supreme Court on Right to Privacy.

directives.meaning: look closely at the facts and issues

scenes.vo: Read what it asks. Examine means weigh, and give a balanced view. There are four jobs. Say what the judgment decided. Show how it widens the scope. Say who is bound, and the limits. Then weigh it.

spec.title: How the Privacy Judgment Widened Fundamental Rights

lines.text: In August twenty seventeen, nine judges signed one order.
Privacy is protected under Article twenty-one.
Two older cases, Sharma and Kharak Singh, were overruled on that point.

scenes.vo: Start with the decision. In August twenty seventeen, nine judges signed one order. Privacy is protected under Article twenty-one. Two older cases, Sharma and Kharak Singh, were overruled on that point.
scenes.visual: Nine chairs and a signed order card; two old case cards stamped 'overruled'.

spec.title: How the Privacy Judgment Widened Fundamental Rights

lines.text: But how can a court add a right?
It says it did not add one.
Fundamental rights are recognised, not granted.

scenes.vo: But how can a court add a right? It says it did not add one. Fundamental rights are recognised, not granted. Life and liberty are inalienable. The Court only recognised what was there.
scenes.visual: A seed inside a closed box labelled Article 21; the lid lifts. Quote card: 'not creations of the Constitution'.

spec.title: How the Privacy Judgment Widened Fundamental Rights

lines.text: That changes the shape of Part III.
In nineteen fifty, Gopalan treated rights as separate silos.
Puttaswamy confirmed it, and overruled ADM Jabalpur.

scenes.vo: That changes the shape of Part III. In nineteen fifty, Gopalan treated rights as separate silos. Later cases made them overlap. Puttaswamy confirmed it, and overruled ADM Jabalpur.

lines.text: Privacy covers dignity, family life, procreation and sexual orientation.
It reaches informational privacy and self-identity.
It binds the State and private actors.

scenes.vo: And the content grows. Privacy covers dignity, family life, procreation and sexual orientation. It reaches informational privacy and self-identity. It binds the State and private actors.

spec.title: How the Privacy Judgment Widened Fundamental Rights

lines.text: A law that invades privacy must have legality, a legitimate aim, and proportionality.
In twenty eighteen the Aadhaar case applied a four-part version of that test.

scenes.vo: But it is not unlimited. A law that invades privacy must have legality, a legitimate aim, and proportionality. In twenty eighteen the Aadhaar case applied a four-part version of that test.
scenes.visual: Three gates; a fourth gate slides in for the Aadhaar test (pay-off of the plant).

blocks.text: On 24 Aug 2017 nine judges held in _Puttaswamy_ that privacy is protected under Article 21 and Part III, overruling M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh.
1. Scope widened

• _Recognised, not granted_: life and liberty are 'inalienable' and inhere in each individual. • _Overlap_: Gopalan's 'silos' gave way to overlapping rights (Cooper, Maneka); ADM Jabalpur was overruled. • _Evolving_: the Constitution 'must evolve with the felt necessities of time'. • New content: dignity, family life, procreation, sexual orientation, informational privacy and self-identity (NALSA). • Koushal's 'so-called' rights view fell; _Navtej Johar_ (2018) followed.
2. Who is bound, and the limits

• Privacy runs against the State and _non-State actors_ (Kaul J.); the Court commended a data-protection regime, now the DPDP Act, 2023. • Not absolute: _legality, need, proportionality_, with Article 21 procedure fair, just and reasonable. • The Aadhaar judgment (2018) applied a four-part proportionality test.
A timeline: Gopalan's silos, then Maneka's overlap, then Puttaswamy, then 2018's cases.
blocks.label: Fig. 1: From silos to privacy

blocks.text: 3. Weighing it

• The Court was 'not amending the Constitution' but recognising a right already there. • The Court did not list every entitlement, so each new facet is settled case by case. • Gain: a base for later dignity cases, such as _Navtej Johar_ and Aadhaar; cost: an open-ended list.
So Part III is wider and still growing, but never absolute: each new facet must pass legality, need and proportionality.

scenes.vo: Now we write. Two hundred and fifty words, about eleven minutes. Open with the date, the nine judges and the two cases overruled. That frames the whole answer.

it must pass legality, need and proportionality

Gopalan's silos were replaced by overlapping rights

weak.text: (no mention of dignity or the 2018 cases)

heads: 2. Who is bound, and the limits

scenes.vo: Now the easy answer beside it. It says the Court amended Article twenty-one. It did not. It says privacy is absolute. It is not. It says only the State is bound. Kaul J. said otherwise. And it repeats the silos idea that the Court replaced.
